niche.title: Can a Tiger I Fire a Tiger II Shell?
niche.description:
Could the Tiger I use ammunition from the Tiger II?

Both German heavy tanks were armed with 88mm guns, but their ammunition was not interchangeable.

The Tiger I used the 8.8 cm KwK 36 L/56 with a 571mm cartridge case, while the Tiger II used the more powerful 8.8 cm KwK 43 L/71 with a longer 822mm case.

The Tiger II's larger cartridge could not fully fit inside the Tiger I's gun chamber.

This 3D animation demonstrates why two tanks with the same gun caliber required different ammunition.

How does a tank shoot down a rocket that's already flying at it? Meet Trophy, the active protection system on this M1A2 Abrams.

Step by step:
• Four flat radar panels watch all around the tank
• An RPG is fired from about 100 meters; its motor lights and pushes it to nearly 300 m/s
• The radar tracks it and the computer predicts its path: will it hit?
• A launcher swings round, aims ahead of the rocket and fires at just the right moment
• The burst tears the rocket apart a few meters from the tank

Launch to intercept: under one second. Trophy only fires when a threat would actually hit, then

niche.title: Why the M1 Abrams Tank Doesn't Eject Brass Casings! #shorts
niche.description:
The M1 Abrams is a powerful American main battle tank armed with a 120mm smoothbore cannon.
Unlike conventional ammunition with fully metallic casings, its main gun uses combustible-case ammunition. Most of the casing burns during firing, leaving a metal base behind. This helps reduce loose debris inside the cramped turret, where the crew operates the gun and handles ammunition. The design supports safer, more efficient operation in a confined space.

Disclaimer: This video is for educational purposes only.

niche.title: Why Do some Tanks Lift Their Guns After Every Shot?  #militarytech #military #3danimation #tank
niche.description:
Why do tanks lift their guns after every shot? They're not aiming at anything. Each gun lets go of its target on purpose. Explained in 3D.

A Leopard 2's gun is stabilized, so inside the turret the breech swings up and down on every bump → nobody can load a moving target with a 44+ lb round → so the gun unlocks from the target and locks to the turret: muzzle up, breech down, dead still → round in, breech shut, and the gun drops right back on target.

A good loader does all this every 8 seconds. Russian tanks like the T-90 do it too, but for a robot autoloader.
